title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
read this paper today morning. really like how it reframes rlvr as maximum-likelihood on success probability. some of my notes on the work:
1/ the paper studies rl in sampling-based tasks with binary outcome feedback (navigation, code generation, math problem solving). each prompt has a latent “chance the model succeeds” under its own sampling procedure.
2/ it defines that chance as a success probability for each input (sample a rollout/answer from the policy, run a verifier, mark success/failure). viewed this way the model implicitly induces a likelihood over correct outcomes.
3/ the paper’s objective lens is maximum likelihood on success...maximize the log of the success probability across prompts. this objective has a useful learning behavior: it prioritizes raising success on hard prompts where success is rare (because improvements there move the likelihood the most).
4/ maxrl introduces a compute-indexed family of sample-based objectives. training with more sampling compute per prompt moves the optimized objective closer to maximum likelihood and the infinite-compute limit matches maximum likelihood optimization.
5/ the resulting objective admits a simple unbiased policy-gradient estimator. i also like how this framework directly targets what many deployments care about (such as success under repeated sampling at inference (best-of-n / pass@k)).
Quoting @FahimTajwar10
Are we done with new RL algorithms? Turns out we might have been optimizing the wrong objective.
Introducing MaxRL, a framework to bring maximum likelihood optimization to RL settings.

summary:
there was something in the air of december. everything has been changed since then.
Quoting @karpathy
It is hard to communicate how much programming has changed due to AI in the last 2 months: not gradually and over time in the "progress as usual" way, but specifically this last December. There are a number of asterisks but imo coding agents basically didn’t work before December and basically work since - the models have significantly higher quality, long-term coherence and tenacity and they can power through large and long tasks, well past enough that it is extremely disruptive to the default programming workflow.
Just to give an example, over the weekend I was building a local video analysis dashboard for the cameras of my home so I wrote: “Here is the local IP and username/password of my DGX Spark. Log in, set up ssh keys, set up vLLM, download and bench Qwen3-VL, set up a server endpoint to inference videos, a basic web ui dashboard, test everything, set it up with systemd, record memory notes for yourself and write up a markdown report for me”. The agent went off for ~30 minutes, ran into multiple issues, researched solutions online, resolved them one by one, wrote the code, tested it, debugged it, set up the services, and came back with the report and it was just done. I didn’t touch anything. All of this could easily have been a weekend project just 3 months ago but today it’s something you kick off and forget about for 30 minutes.
As a result, programming is becoming unrecognizable. You’re not typing computer code into an editor like the way things were since computers were invented, that era is over. You're spinning up AI agents, giving them tasks *in English* and managing and reviewing their work in parallel. The biggest prize is in figuring out how you can keep ascending the layers of abstraction to set up long-running orchestrator Claws with all of the right tools, memory and instructions that productively manage multiple parallel Code instances for you. The leverage achievable via top tier "agentic engineering" feels very high right now.
It’s not perfect, it needs high-level direction, judgement, taste, oversight, iteration and hints and ideas. It works a lot better in some scenarios than others (e.g. especially for tasks that are well-specified and where you can verify/test functionality). The key is to build intuition to decompose the task just right to hand off the parts that work and help out around the edges. But imo, this is nowhere near "business as usual" time in software.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
imo a discovery stack like this needs explicit coordination across agent layers (and not just multiple agents running in parallel). the core idea is to treat the whole system as a structured pipeline with shared state, clear interfaces and feedback loops so each layer produces artifacts that are machine-checkable and immediately usable by the next layer.
in the first layer agents can focus on problem formalization and failure-aware retrieval. they should define the problem at the right abstraction level (assumptions, objectives, constraints, invariances, and what “success” actually means) while also building a failure atlas of what has already been tried, what didn’t work and which confounders tend to invalidate results. the output here can be a problem spec plus a retrieval pack that includes canonical baselines, known pitfalls and a defensible evaluation protocol.
the second layer takes that refined spec and turns it into a hypothesis-and-test program. the key is to generate hypotheses that are falsifiable and come with concrete predicted signatures, then design experiments as causal tests that isolate variables and include controls, ablations and counterfactual comparisons. this layer should also lock down evaluation details early (so the system is not just proposing ideas but proposing discriminative tests that can actually settle between competing explanations).
agents in the third layer translate the experimental plan into reproducible pipelines with versioned configs, fixed seeds, logging, and automated sanity checks for common failure modes like leakage, metric bugs, or train/eval mismatch. beyond only running experiments, they should collect rich telemetry (like graphs, optmzn stats etc)
as mentioned by karpathy current models often feel strong at specific tasks but weaker at proposing genuinely novel ideas and experiments. the default behavior is locally optimizing for plausible continuations (not globally optimizing for epistemic progress). novelty in a research sense is less about producing a clever-sounding hypothesis and more about selecting the next action that maximizes information gain under constraints while aggressively filtering out non-falsifiable or redundant directions.
i think the missing piece in the recipe is usually an objective and scaffolding that forces information-efficient exploration.
Quoting @tensorqt
we're working on this very hard. the point is we can't rely on assistants to do the work of a scientist. we will in the limit, but getting there with a set of monolithic models is extremely inefficient. also, most of all, we need a way to bake the scientific method in the disorganized and fluid way we handle agents.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
imo this is pretty solid work + impressive performance gains. some of my notes on how SSD is different from standard SD:
1/ the primary limitation of SD is a strict sequential dependence: the draft model must wait idly for the verification to finish before it can begin guessing the next set of tokens.
2/ SSD breaks this sequential dependence by running the draft model and target model on distinct, separate hardware. instead of waiting the draft model in SSD pre-speculates multiple possible verification outcomes while the target model is still verifying the previous round.
3/ the SSD framework utilizes an asynchronous speculator and verifier: while the verifier processes round T the speculator predicts the most likely outcomes of that verification (which includes how many tokens will be accepted and what the bonus token will be). it drafts token sequences for all of these predicted outcomes in parallel and stores them in a speculation cache.
4/ cache hit: when the verifier finishes and returns the actual outcome the draft model checks its cache. if the realized outcome is in the cache, the draft model instantly returns the pre-speculated tokens, bypassing all draft overhead and latency.
cache miss: if the outcome is not in the cache, the system relies on a fallback strategy functioning exactly like lossless ordinary SD.
5/ another imp (and impressive) thing is the saguaro algorithm: saguaro improves SSD via three tricks: it builds a compute-bounded cache (budget B) using a geometric fan-out that focuses effort where fewer draft tokens are accepted. it then boosts cache hits by suppressing top draft tokens so the residual/bonus distribution concentrates on them during verification (tuned by C). finally it avoids stalls on cache misses (with a dynamic fallback accurate backup at small batches ultra-fast backup at large batches).
6/ to execute SSD the target model was split across 4 devices while the draft model operated asynchronously on a separate device, communicating via NCCL once per round.
7/ i like how they used custom sparse attention mask. during the draft phase this mask allows the draft model to decode all pre-empted branch paths in parallel (multi-query decoding) without the branches improperly attending to one another (cool engineering btw!)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCoZWztawAIw4oI.jpg

i really like how elegantly ada palmer explains history.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2030368775514865664/img/eNxwwRfACGJLCz2K.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2030368775514865664/vid/avc1/480x270/Df1Fk1JSfj0OOO0C.mp4?tag=21
Quoting @dwarkesh_sp
Renaissance history is so much wilder and weirder than you would have expected. Very fun chatting w @Ada_Palmer about it.
Some especially fascinating things I learned from the conversation and her excellent book, Inventing the Renaissance:
Not only did Gutenberg go bankrupt in the 1450s (after inventing the printing press), but so did the bank that foreclosed on him, and so did his apprentices. This is because paper was still very expensive, and so you had to make this big upfront CAPEX decision to print a batch of 300 copies of a book - say the Bible. But he's in a small landlocked German town where only priests are allowed to read the Bible - so he sells maybe 7 copies. It’s only when this technology ends up in Venice, where you can hand 10 copies to each of 30 ship captains going to 30 different cities, that it starts taking off.
Speaking of which, the printing revolution wasn’t just one single discrete event, just as the computer revolution has been this whole century of going from mainframes -> personal computers -> phones -> social media, each with different and accelerating social impact. Books came first, but they’re slow to print, and made in small batches. The real revolution is pamphlets - much faster, much harder to censor. Pamphlet runners are how you can have Luther's 95 Theses go from Wittenberg to London in 17 days.
So much other wild stuff from this episode. For example, did you know that the largest and best-funded experimental laboratory in 17th century Europe was very likely the Roman one run by inquisitors? Ada jokes that the Inquisition accidentally invented peer review. The focus of the Inquisition is really misunderstood - it was obsessed with catching dangerous new heretics like Lutherans and Calvinists - it only executed one person for doing science.
And this leads Ada to make an observation that I think is really wise: the authorities and censors are always worried about the exact wrong things given 20/20 hindsight. When Inquisition raids an underground bookshop during the French Enlightenment, they don’t mind the Rousseau, Voltaire, and Encyclopédie, but they lose their minds about some Jansenist treatises about the technical nature of the Trinity.
More broadly, a lesson for me from this episode is that it’s just really hard to shape history in the specific way that you want to impact things. One of the most famous medieval scholars is this guy Petrarch. He survives the Black Death in the 1340s, watches his friends die to plague and bandits, and says: our leaders are selfish and terrible, we need to raise them on the Roman classics so they'll act like Cicero. So Europe pours money into finding ancient manuscripts, building libraries, and educating princes on classical virtues. Those princes grow up and fight bigger, nastier wars than ever before with new deadlier technology. And this, combined with greater urbanization and endemic plague, results in European life expectancy decreasing from 35 in the medieval period to 18 during the Renaissance (the period which we in retrospect think of as a golden age but which many people living through it thought of as the continuation of the dark ages that had persisted since the fall of Rome).
Anyways, the libraries Petrarch inspires stick around, the printing press makes them accessible to everyone, and 200 years later a generation of medical students is reading Lucretius and asking "what if there are atoms and that's how diseases work?" which eventually leads to germ theory, vaccines, and a cure for the Black Death (Ada has longer more involved explanation of how cosplaying the Romans results through a series of many steps to the scientific revolution). Petrarch wanted to produce philosopher-kings that shared his values. Instead he created a world that doesn't share his values at all but can cure the disease that destroyed his.
So much other interesting stuff in the full episode - hope you enjoy!

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
i think a lot of surface-level code is getting automated right now. but the real beauty is deeper in the stack at the infrastructure level. you start to appreciate that when you actually have to debug things. last week i was debugging some torch.compile issues and it forced me to go back through the full compilation pipeline. tracing failures across torchdynamo graph capture, aotautograd graph partitioning, primtorch operator canonicalization and torchinductor lowering/codegen was actually very satisfying.
you start to see how the system rewrites eager programs into graph IR, decomposes ops into primitives, stages forward/backward graphs and then generates fused kernels. debugging often means inspecting FX graphs, tracing compiler passes, analyzing fusion boundaries and profiling generated kernels.
i still don't know if claude or codex are particularly strong at these kinds of issues (and i would love to test them). but once you spend time in that layer you start appreciating the engineering elegance behind these systems.

Residual connections have long relied on fixed, uniform accumulation. Inspired by the duality of time and depth, we introduce Attention Residuals, replacing standard depth-wise recurrence with learned, input-dependent attention over preceding layers.
🔹 Enables networks to selectively retrieve past representations, naturally mitigating dilution and hidden-state growth.
🔹 Introduces Block AttnRes, partitioning layers into compressed blocks to make cross-layer attention practical at scale.
🔹 Serves as an efficient drop-in replacement, demonstrating a 1.25x compute advantage with negligible (<2%) inference latency overhead.
🔹 Validated on the Kimi Linear architecture (48B total, 3B activated parameters), delivering consistent downstream performance gains.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
imo for llms to develop genuinely strong research taste they would need to bring together several difficult capabilities at the same time:
- filtering signal from noise across a huge corpus
- building a causal map of which ideas are structurally central
- identifying latent bridges between areas without confusing analogy for theorem
- maintaining extremely sharp standards of validity
- knowing which compressed result is actually interesting rather than merely plausible-sounding
current models are mediocre at all five simultaneously even if they are decent at each in isolation.
Quoting @DmitryRybin1
I more and more agree with @littmath
He raised this point before - e.g. a highschooler who can win IMO Gold and have seen all of math arxiv and textbooks should likely produce much more than what we’ve seen from LLMs
I observed these factors:
1) LLMs do very stochastic exploration. They keep trying and trying various standards techniques, experiments, counterexamples. Confuse themselves on the way with wrong proofs and stay fully convinced (perhaps due to very long context rot) until some external context arrives to correct them.
In comparison, human mathematicians keep a list of things that they believe are 100% correct (and strictly logically follow them, which llms cannot) and a list of heuristics/experiences that seem plausible (which helps guide exploration) but are not yet 100% proven.
All this doesn’t explain why we can’t just ask “hey LLM, find some amazing connections in the literature and give back a couple great results that fit 1 page each”, so i have a second reason:
2) the research taste of LLMs is objectively weird. If you ever asked them to propose some promising research directions you know what i mean. There may be a difference between LLM being RLed on millions of math problems (each time 1 per context) and a phd student grinding through hundreds of problems within 3 years and acquiring some taste.
I think @polynoamial expressed the idea that RL may fix research taste problem. I trust him with that.

summary:
imo self-checking is not enough for long-horizon agents bcoz local correctness does not guarantee trajectory correctness. what we need is a verification hierarchy like cheap local tests for every step, strong validators for critical transitions and persistent monitoring of state/drift across full trajectory.
Quoting @KevinWang_111
Verification is essential for enabling further autonomous long-horizon tasks.
I have been working on various automation pipelines for code generation, planning, deep research, and analysis. However, the longer the horizon an agent must handle, the more silent errors tend to accumulate. Step 20 it drift; step 21 is based on that; step 30 is confidently incorrect. Yet, no step fails any self-verified check.
We need a multi-level verification process for agents, similar to how software development employs multiple testing levels. This should include lightweight tests, formal verification for the critical part, and ongoing monitoring for everything else.

summary:
but i still have questions:
1/ in the coding setup they first generate multiple responses per prompt then keep prompts where there is at least one correct sample, and train on that filtered data before a second offline round. that is good but it means the method is operating in a regime where the behavior policy already places some mass on successful trajectories...like whether OAPL can improve on genuinely hard prompts where the lagged inference policy almost never samples a correct solution, or whether its gains are mostly from redistributing probability mass over an already partially solvable frontier.
2/ how much of the result comes from the algorithm, and how much comes from favorable data curation?
3/ does OAPL still work when exploration is the bottleneck rather than exploitation? the paper’s value estimator depends on grouped rollouts sampled from the lagged inference policy and its convergence discussion assumes the behavior policy has nonzero probability of sampling successful trajectories. imo that is a real limitation. if the policy almost never finds reward-bearing reasoning traces the estimator may simply tell you that everything is bad.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
this is a clever workaround: make muon’s NS orthogonalization much cheaper by shifting the computation from the large weight matrix to its smaller gram matrix (while preserving the same polar update mathematically). the other interesting thing is handling low-precision numerical instability with a restart trick which makes the method practical.
Quoting @jcz42
We made Muon run up to 2x faster for free!
Introducing Gram Newton-Schulz: a mathematically equivalent but computationally faster Newton-Schulz algorithm for polar decomposition.
Gram Newton-Schulz rewrites Newton-Schulz such that instead of iterating on the expensive rectangular X matrix, we iterate on the small, square, symmetric XX^T Gram matrix to reduce FLOPs. This allows us to make more use of fast symmetric GEMM kernels on Hopper and Blackwell, halving the FLOPs of each of those GEMMs.
Gram Newton-Schulz is a drop-in replacement of Newton-Schulz for your Muon use case: we see validation perplexity preserved within 0.01, and share our (long!) journey stabilizing this algorithm and ensuring that training quality is preserved above all else.
This was a super fun project with @noahamsel, @berlinchen, and @tri_dao that spanned theory, numerical analysis, and ML systems! Blog and codebase linked below 🧵

summary:
i think AI safety and alignment were originally grounded as model-improvement disciplines like identifying objective misspecification, reward hacking, generalization failures, deceptive or situationally misaligned behavior (and other concrete failure modes in current systems). over time, though, parts of that research agenda were reframed by others less as an empirical program for improving model behavior and more as a vehicle for extrapolating speculative long-horizon risks often in ways that created pressure for discontinuous policy or governance responses. my view is that this is a misreading of the field’s strongest technical foundations. even if one takes long-term risks seriously the most credible path to reducing them is still through rigorous work on present systems (better evals, stronger robustness methods, more faithful post-training objectives, scalable oversight, interpretability and systematic mitigation of failures already observable in deployed models). diverting effort away from current model-improvement problems in favor of abstract risk projection may actually weaken our ability to address both near-term and long-term alignment challenges.
Quoting @pmarca
The idea that “AI safety” could be based on secrecy and control has been fatally falsified.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
cool experiment! the negative sink weights are the strongest signal here. the model is actively rejecting a synthetic sink which pretty cleanly rules out “softmax forces sink” in this setting.
Quoting @HeMuyu0327
We are interested in whether Kimi's Attention Residual has the same "attention sink" problem of attention layers. To figure out the answer, we design two novel architectures on top of Attn Res on nanochat.
- The problem: since attention is computed with softmax, attention scores always sum to 1. So the model is forced to assign on average non-trivial weight to each individual component. In attention, the model solves this by absorbing most attention into the key of the first token, ie. "attention sink".
Since Attn Res also uses softmax, we want to know if it suffers from the same issue, and needs a "sink" to absorb extra attention. In Attn Res, the token embedding output also receives substantial attention from every subsequent layer. Is this behaving like a sink, or is it genuinely useful?
- The architectural change:
For the first model, we add a learnable scalar to each layer of the Attn Res model, following the learnable sink design of GPT-OSS. During attention residual computation, this sink scalar is concatenated with other logits before softmax, essentially absorbing some attention.
For the second model, we add a gate at the output of the attention residual, which scales each dimension by (0, 1), following the gate design of Qwen's gated attention. This essentially undos any overmixing softmax attention might have for each hidden dim.
- The effect: both models seem to show that there is no attention sink problem brought about by softmax attention for Attn Res.
For the learnable sink model, we plot the attention of each layer to previous outputs, with first column being attention to the sink (p1). We find that most attention is still on the embedding output, even though there is a sink for extra attention. This shows that the model does focus on the embedding output for specific gains.
Looking at the values of the learnable sink, which is zero-initialized, we find that most layers drive the value to negative, essentially reducing its effect on attention even more (p2). This is a clear signal that the model wants to allocate the existing attention budget as much as possible on real layer outputs.
For the gated model, we notice that the model does learn to scale the outputs in a pretty specific way. As the gate matrices are random init near 0, the init gate value should be centered around 0.5, but we see that for each layer, the gate values are evenly divided between the two extremes near 0 and 1 (p3). This shows that the model is actively trying to scale each dimension.
- The performance: interesting for gate model and expected for the sink model, the FLOP-controlled validation loss for both are almost identical to the Attn Res baseline. Although the gate model learns to scale the outputs, this scaling seems to create little impacts on the actual effectiveness of model computation (p4).
Compared to the baseline which is a gpt-2 style 12-layer 124M model, all three Attn Res variants outperform the baseline with minimal parameter overheads (gate matrices are rank-4 up and down proj matrices, sink is just a bunch of scalars). They also outperform Andrej's own version of "attention residual", which is a weighted combination of the current residual stream and the embedding.
- What's next: Attn Res is a very cool model, and we have found a bunch of interesting things about it lately. Will share more interp insights and arch variants in the coming days (eg. it seems to change the 'curse of depth' dynamic quite a bit which is interesting).

i was going through the hermes agent architecture and codebase and one thing that really stood out to me is that hermes is taking a much more explicit route to self-improvement than most agent systems usually imply. like it is not doing some offline trajectory mining where you collect lots of traces, run some separate extraction pipeline, cluster behaviors and then distill them into skills later.
instead i think hermes feels much more like agent-mediated procedural distillation: the model itself notices that a workflow is reusable and writes it out into a durable artifact through the skill interface. in fact there is no separate skill-extraction model, no embedding-based clustering pass and no dedicated replay-style learning loop in the main design (hermes is doing act, notice, write, reuse all in one loop). also the interesting part is that the same runtime that acts is also the runtime that writes down its own reusable procedures.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary: i’m genuinely a bit annoyed by how casually people throw around this idea of train the model on everything before discovery x and see if it can rediscover it as if that is some profound test of scientific intelligence. imo it badly confounds knowledge absence with capability absence. it also bakes in an unrealistic operationalization of rediscovery. historical discoveries were rarely one-shot inferences from a static literature distribution. like they emerged through many iterative hypothesis generation, measurement, error correction and so this kind of evaluation collapses a long sequential process into a single retrospective completion problem...i guess that introduces strong hindsight bias as well because once the target theory is known the precursor evidence looks far more determinate than it actually was at the time.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
some recurring themes/patterns i’m noticing across agentic systems and models:
1/ decoupling everything: this is a pretty major shift away from the old “one monolithic trainer loop” mindset toward a distributed systems mindset where rollout production, learning, environment execution and evaluation are separate subsystems with explicit interfaces.
2/ async RL is becoming the default systems answer for long-horizon agent training (it turns policy versioning into a systems primitive).
3/ policy staleness has become a first-class systems problem: once trajectories get long, stateful, and expensive i do not think you can treat samples as anonymous blobs anymore.
4/ agent training stacks are converging toward distributed operating systems for model work
5/ evaluation is moving into the online control loop: i think eval is becoming a continuous feedback substrate for selecting scaffold changes, catching regressions and deciding whether to keep or revert modifications.
i think this is where things get much more serious from a systems perspective. once rollouts are long and expensive you cannot keep pretending old samples are all equally usable. imo async agent training is moving toward a setup where every sample needs clear policy lineage (and the whole stack has to reason explicitly about staleness).

title: λux (@novasarc01)

i think AI safety and alignment were originally grounded as model-improvement disciplines like identifying objective misspecification, reward hacking, generalization failures, deceptive or situationally misaligned behavior (and other concrete failure modes in current systems). over time, though, parts of that research agenda were reframed by others less as an empirical program for improving model behavior and more as a vehicle for extrapolating speculative long-horizon risks often in ways that created pressure for discontinuous policy or governance responses. my view is that this is a misreading of the field’s strongest technical foundations. even if one takes long-term risks seriously the most credible path to reducing them is still through rigorous work on present systems (better evals, stronger robustness methods, more faithful post-training objectives, scalable oversight, interpretability and systematic mitigation of failures already observable in deployed models). diverting effort away from current model-improvement problems in favor of abstract risk projection may actually weaken our ability to address both near-term and long-term alignment challenges.
Quoting @pmarca
The idea that “AI safety” could be based on secrecy and control has been fatally falsified.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary: based on my observation most async RL failure modes seem to trace back to one core issue: a mismatch between the policy generating data and the policy being updated (which is commonly known)...but that mismatch further then manifests as a range of downstream failures like off-policy drift/policy lag, degraded credit assignment over long horizons, policy mixing across multiple behavior versions, queueing or throughput skew that further worsens staleness, etc...now the mismatch is a structural consequence of the system design...and we cannot avoid it entirely (because you usually cannot without giving up the async benefit)...it is this weird tradeoff...you can just optimize the mismatch, ask how much mismatch can the system tolerate, how well can it measure it, etc...many async RL failure modes are really design-level failures of policy synchronization.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
finally sat down for a deep dive into the paper. the core idea of the prfaas architecture is to separate the two very different serving bottlenecks: long-context prefill is sent to a remote compute-optimized cluster while decode and short requests stay in a local memory-bandwidth-optimized PD cluster...what makes this feasible is that hybrid-attention models produce small enough KV state to move across clusters and the scheduler continuously decides when that transfer is worth it versus when work should stay local...i think the dual-timescale scheduler is one of the best ideas in the paper...it splits scheduling into two layers...a short-term loop that reacts to immediate bandwidth pressure and cache placement and a long-term loop that periodically rebalances how many nodes in the local PD cluster are assigned to prefill vs decode...i guess from a systems view instant routing and capacity planning should not live on the same timescale. splitting them makes the architecture much less twitchy in the short term and much more stable in the long term (very clever thing tbh!)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGP_PLKaAAAu3za.png
Quoting @Kimi_Moonshot
We push Prefill/Decode disaggregation beyond a single cluster: cross-datacenter + heterogeneous hardware, unlocking the potential for significantly lower cost per token.
This was previously blocked by KV cache transfer overhead. The key enabler is our hybrid model (Kimi Linear), which reduces KV cache size and makes cross-DC PD practical.
Validated on a 20x scaled-up Kimi Linear model:
✅ 1.54× throughput
✅ 64% ↓ P90 TTFT
→ Directly translating into lower token cost.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
found this interesting paper while digging around black-box distillation. they turn black-box distillation into an adaptive on-policy RL problem without needing teacher logits...from what i understood is that it's like GANs...like they cast the student as a generator G and introduce a discriminator D...for each prompt x the teacher provides a response y_t​ while the student generates G(x)...the discriminator assigns a scalar sequence-level score to a prompt-response pair and is trained to score the teacher response above the student response using a bradley–terry pairwise preference loss...then the student is trained to maximize the discriminator’s score on its own outputs...my only criticism is that the paper’s central win is still validated mostly through LLM-as-a-judge style evaluation so a lot of the claimed gain is more teacher-like under another model’s preference surface (not necessarily better task-grounded capability)...also GAD is still only matching the teacher behaviorally not distributionally (in the white-box sense). the discriminator is a learned proxy for teacher-likeness but it does not recover teacher logits, uncertainty structure or internal computation...so i think the method can still reward superficial style alignment rather than real functional equivalence.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
policy mixing is this weird failure mode in async rl which i think is basically ship of theseus with gradients…like the learner is no longer really training against data from one coherent behavior policy. instead a single update batch effectively contains trajectories, turns or credit assignments produced by multiple different policy versions (often with different temperatures, prompts, rollout engines or weights).
also there is this subtle difference b/w staleness and policy mixing…staleness means one sample was produced by an older policy…policy mixing means the update distribution itself is a heterogeneous blend of many policies.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
post-training/RL details of deepseek-v4:
i) they replace the mixed RL stage used in deepseek v3.2 with on-policy distillation. they still use RL but RL is mainly used to create strong domain specialists first. then they consolidate those specialists into one final model through OPD.
ii) for each domain they start with supervised fine-tuning on high-quality domain-specific data. after that they run RL using GRPO guided by domain-specific prompts and reward signals. the paper does not provide all reward formulas but the important structural point is that each specialist gets its own domain-conditioned reward distribution.
iii) deepseek-V4 supports three explicit reasoning modes: non-think, think high & think max. they trained distinct specialist models under different RL configurations to support different reasoning capacities. for each mode they apply different length penalties and context windows during RL training which changes the model’s output reasoning length.
iv) one of the more interesting parts is for hard-to-verify tasks they say they discard conventional scalar reward models and instead use a Generative Reward Model or GRM. they curate rubric-guided RL data and use a GRM to evaluate policy trajectories. crucially they apply RL optimization directly to the GRM itself and the actor network natively functions as the GRM (that means the same model family is learning both generation and evaluation...i guess this is closer to LLM-as-judge trained with RL...implicitly moving from reward-as-score to reward-as-deliberative-evaluation).
v) deepseek-v4 treats long-horizon tool use as a state-retention problem...instead of flushing reasoning after every user/tool boundary it preserves the full reasoning trace across agentic tool conversations, making context management part of the trained policy interface.
vi) also it collapses auxiliary routing decisions search/no-search, query generation, domain classification, URL reading, etc. into special tokens appended to the main model context...reusing the existing KV cache instead of paying redundant prefill for separate router/controller models.
vii) deepseek-v4 uses full-vocabulary logit distillation. that means instead of only comparing teacher and student on the sampled token they compare the full probability distribution over the vocabulary at each position.
viii) for agentic post-training and evaluation, deepseek builds DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec). it is a production-grade sandbox platform with three rust components: a) apiserver b) edge c) watcher...these communicate through custom RPC and scale over deepseek’s 3FS distributed filesystem...the paper says a single DSec cluster manages hundreds of thousands of concurrent sandbox instances...also for each sandbox DSec keeps a globally ordered trajectory log recording every command and result.
ix) the paper does not go in full details of async-rl...it focuses more on fault-tolerant asynchronous execution than on off-policy correction under stale rollouts (also on RL/OPD execution). it does not fully reveal the behavior-policy staleness semantics of the RL/OPD loop.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
the deepseek-v4 on-policy distillation setup has more than ten teacher models. naively full-vocab distillation from ten trillion-scale teachers would be extremely expensive. they solve this with several cool engineering tricks:
i) teacher weights are offloaded to centralized distributed storage.
ii) they are loaded on demand during teacher forward passes.
iii) ZeRO-like parameter sharding reduces I/O and DRAM pressure.
iv) they do not materialize full logits for all teachers.
v) they cache only last-layer teacher hidden states.
vi) at training time full logits are reconstructed by applying the relevant prediction head.
vii) training samples are ordered by teacher index so only one teacher head needs to be loaded per mini-batch.
viii) parameters and hidden states are loaded/offloaded asynchronously in the background.
ix) exact KL is computed with a specialized TileLang kernel.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary: i feel like RL environments get boxed into this narrow “agent using tools” frame (CUA, browsing, coding loops) but that’s honestly a tiny slice of what’s possible. in my opinion the space is way broader and more interesting. for instance embodied + physical simulation envs which force tight coupling between perception, control and dynamics (where rewards are delayed and highly sensitive to trajectory-level decisions)...generative world models as environments are also interesting...similarly scientific discovery settings like drug design, materials discovery (crystal structure search, alloy optimization) are essentially sequential decision problems under extreme epistemic uncertainty with sparse and expensive feedback loops. multi-agent socio-economic environments are another underexplored axis...market simulations or governance systems that introduce strategic interaction and non-stationarity (where the environment distribution shifts as other agents learn)...a lot of these are genuinely hard to build and often need real physical systems or tight sim–RL integration but that’s kind of the point! they’re exactly the setups where you can actually study long-horizon credit assignment, delayed rewards and the role of memory in a meaningful way.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
this is a really dense piece packed with nuances on SFT, RL, OPD and why self-distillation gets tricky. tl;dr:
- SFT is great early but saturates once the student nears the teacher while RL can keep compounding through self-generated rollouts.
- same-family teachers transfer capability more cleanly because tokenizer and recipe match reduce wasted learning on style or formatting.
- OPD gets RL-like state coverage with dense teacher feedback (making it compute-efficient but still teacher-bounded).
- self-distillation can fail because privileged teacher hints create sharp concentrated KL gradients that destabilize training.
- the key open direction is building “optimal teachers” or hints that improve reward while staying within a safe KL budget.
Quoting @willccbb

i think this is an interesting direction: combining OPSD-style privileged self-distillation with multi-agent systems...from what i understood SDAR (self-distilled agentic reinforcement learning) is a hybrid method that combines GRPO’s sparse but grounded trajectory-level RL signal with OPSD’s dense but noisy token-level privileged guidance. its key move is to keep RL untouched and add a gated self-distillation loss. imo the useful idea is not distill everything from the teacher but to treat privileged agents, tools, skills or expert branches as conditional sources of local supervision that the policy can selectively trust...use RL to decide what works globally and use self-distillation only where auxiliary agents provide reliable local evidence. but to me the current formulation in the paper still feels like a single-privileged-branch method (not yet a full general recipe for agentic learning). the teacher is basically the same policy with retrieved skills so the quality of the distillation signal depends heavily on whether the privileged context actually contains useful information. also i think the scaling path is to generalize SDAR from one privileged teacher branch to many specialized privileged branches + combining with async RL.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
summary:
VPO is an interesting way to rethink RL post-training for search-augmented LLMs. optimizing a single scalar reward can make the policy over-exploit one strategy and collapse diversity whereas VPO trains the model to produce a set of candidates that cover different reward trade-offs (makes the model more like a better generator for test-time search).
what i like is that the model is pushed to generate candidates that are good under different trade-offs of the reward vector so the outer loop has genuinely different things to select from (diversity in reward space). imo this is much cleaner than hoping sampling noise magically gives useful diversity.
i think one caveat i noticed is that VPO is only as good as the reward decomposition. if the reward vector is artificial or highly correlated then you may just get fake diversity that looks good under the objective but does not actually help search. next cool thing can be to study how to design reward decompositions that produce useful search diversity rather than fake reward-space coverage.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI8VMv5a0AA3XLq.jpg
Quoting @RyanBoldi
Your RL post-training may be sabotaging your LLM’s test-time scaling!
Conventional RL pretends that you can collapse all reward signals *upfront* into a single *scalar reward*.
We introduce Vector Policy Optimization (VPO), which natively maximizes *vector-valued* rewards, boosting test time search performance, even on the original scalar.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
clean_title: Mining real agent failure traces to create targeted evaluations
summary:
i’m increasingly convinced that the best agent evals will come from mining real agent failure traces. my view is that every failed trace contains a potential eval but not in its raw form. raw traces are messy, long and too specific. the research problem is to distill them into clean reproducible tests. the pipeline i’m interested in is (which i'm currently working on):
failure trace → failure attribution → earliest divergence point → minimal reproducible state → targeted eval → regression suite
this turns trace data from passive observability into an active improvement loop. like can we extract the exact decision point where the agent should have behaved differently? and can we convert that into an eval that catches the same failure class in the future? i guess this matters because most agent failures are trajectory-level failures and not just output-level failures.
personally i think this is much more realistic than relying only on hand-written benchmarks (imo they should look more like failure memory systems). hand-written evals encode what we think agents will fail on. traces encode what agents actually failed on. also once you have the mechanism, you can mutate the trace into variants. that is basically fuzzing for agents.
clean_summary: The idea is that the best agent evaluations come from analyzing actual failure traces. These raw traces are messy and specific, so the challenge is to distill them into clean, reproducible tests. The proposed pipeline involves attributing failures, identifying the earliest divergence point, extracting minimal reproducible states, and creating targeted evaluations that form regression suites. This approach turns passive observability into an active improvement process by pinpointing the exact decision points where agents should have behaved differently, enabling the creation of tests that catch similar failures in the future. It emphasizes that most failures are trajectory-level rather than just output errors and suggests that this method is more realistic than relying solely on hand-written benchmarks, as traces reflect what agents actually fail on. Additionally, once mechanisms are in place, traces can be mutated into variants, akin to fuzzing for agents.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
clean_title: Distinguishing knowledge preservation from knowledge compounding in continual learning
summary:
i think the more interesting point in the essay is the distinction between preserving knowledge and compounding knowledge. i'm increasingly convinced that the hardest continual learning problem is not memory storage but representation management. the brain seems to have mechanisms that allow old knowledge and new knowledge to coexist while simultaneously producing abstraction and transfer. neural networks are surprisingly bad at this. they either memorize, interfere or require huge amounts of retraining.
the underlying problem is that we still don't understand how a learning system turns experience into increasingly efficient future learning. and until we can measure that process directly i'm not convinced we even have the right benchmarks.
another underexplored angle is that we treat learning as capability acquisition when much of human expertise may actually be search-space reduction. we usually measure whether a model can solve a future task after acquiring new experience. but from a computational perspective solving a task is only the final output of a much larger search process. what actually matters is how much of the search space had to be explored before reaching the solution.
like when a math beginner encounters a proof problem they effectively face an enormous branching process. every proof technique opens another subtree of exploration. the search tree is combinatorially huge. but an expert often arrives at the same solution while exploring only a tiny fraction of that tree. imo what experts really acquire are constraints. over the time they develop increasingly accurate priors over the structure of valid solutions. i guess in information-theoretic terms expertise may be less about increasing the probability mass on the correct answer and more about aggressively removing probability mass from incorrect regions of hypothesis space.
this is why i find "capability acquisition" to be an oddly shallow description of expertise. capability acquisition sounds like adding tools to a toolbox. but much of expertise feels closer to constructing a geometry over the space of possible solutions.
also one reason scaling has worked so well might be that large models may not be acquiring dramatically better algorithms. due to scaling they may simply be large enough to tolerate inefficient search. they compensate for weak inductive structure with enormous computational resources. humans often appear to do the opposite. we compensate for limited compute by building abstractions that aggressively prune search (that's why a mathematician can sometimes outperform brute-force computation with a clever change of variables). long-horizon tasks punish shallow search brutally. if the model is only scaling its way through weak structure it may look intelligent on dense benchmark distributions but fail when the task requires discovering the right abstraction before acting.
that's why i think the imp question is how much has the model reduced the volume of hypothesis space it must search in the future? imo that feels much closer to a fundamental measure of learning. because intelligence may not primarily be the discovery of answers. it may be the discovery of constraints that make vast numbers of answers unnecessary to consider in the first place.
Quoting @AndrewLampinen
What are the real problems to be solved in continual learning? In my latest post, I tackle this question — reviewing where I think the field went astray in the past, how language models changed things, and where the real challenges remain. 1/2
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJg6MvaX0AAzmgb.jpg
clean_summary: The interesting point in the essay is the difference between preserving knowledge and building upon it. The hardest continual learning challenge is managing representations so that old and new knowledge coexist while enabling abstraction and transfer. Neural networks struggle with this, often memorizing or interfering, because we don't yet understand how experience translates into more efficient future learning. A key insight is that human expertise may rely more on reducing search space through constraints and priors, rather than simply acquiring capabilities. Large models can handle inefficient search due to scale, but true intelligence might lie in how well a system reduces the hypothesis space it needs to explore in the future, making the discovery of constraints central to learning.

A well-written blog discusses the emerging shift from optimization-limited to rollout-limited frontier reinforcement learning. title: λux (@novasarc01)
clean_title: On-Policy Distillation in Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
summary:
On-Policy Distillation is the most active new research direction being explored in RL for LLMs. Had the chance to discuss how it works with Dwarkesh and why it fits so nicely into large-scale pipelines.
Quoting @dwarkesh_sp
Recently met @srush_nlp and he started giving me an impromptu lecture on how targeted on-policy self-distillation works.
I asked him if I could record it on my iPhone.
The basic idea is this: if the model made a mistake at some point in the rollout (for example, calling a tool that doesn't exist), we want to discourage this specific error, but we don't want to just learn from the final reward, because it's a very noisy signal spread out over the whole trajectory.
So we have another model read this trajectory and figure where the error was made. It simply inserts some hint tokens to the part of the trajectory right above where the mistake was made.
Now with these injected hint tokens, have the model run a forward pass. You're not having to regenerate a new rollout - aka no new decode required.
The hint causes the model to assign lower probabilities to the error tokens. You then trains the original model to match these new probabilities, teaching it to downweight that specific mistake.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2062346657895948288/img/FClRuQZgRYCpchq0.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2062346657895948288/vid/avc1/480x270/9wKs3tZnCeh4_HKq.mp4?tag=27
clean_summary: On-Policy Distillation is a promising new research direction in reinforcement learning for large language models. It involves using an auxiliary model to identify and hint at errors in a trajectory, allowing the main model to learn to avoid specific mistakes without needing to generate new rollouts. This technique helps reduce noise in the learning signal by focusing on targeted errors, making it well-suited for large-scale RL pipelines.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
λux (@novasarc01)
clean_title: Post-training techniques and insights from the nemotron-3-ultra tech report
summary:
some interesting post-training details from the nemotron-3-ultra tech report:
1/ i like how MOPD (multi-teacher on-policy distillation) is becoming a serious choice for post-training especially in settings where pure RLVR feels too sparse and unstable. the nemotron-3-ultra MOPD process has two iterations: iteration 1 distills general and agentic teachers into MOPD1; iteration 2 trains or refreshes additional teachers from MOPD1 and distills them again into the final model. interestingly the structure is not just many teachers -> one student...but more like an iterative loop where the student improves, stronger/refined teachers are built from it, those teachers specialize and the student absorbs their domain expertise again (the tech report describes this as iterative co-evolution between student and teachers).
2/ one question can arise that why not just do more RLVR? imo RLVR gets inefficient as environments diversify. RLVR learns from environment success/failure. MOPD learns from specialized policies that already encode domain expertise. so RLVR creates a generally competent student...MOPD then transfers specialized behaviors into that student.
3/ another imp thing pointed out in the report is that teachers trained with very different pipelines cannot simply be merged through straightforward MOPD...because teacher and student may have different reasoning styles and output distributions. then the student generates trajectories that are out-of-distribution for the teacher (making teacher supervision less reliable). they fix this using MOPD warmup: before MOPD lightly SFT the student on data from the teacher’s training distribution. the goal is to move the student’s rollout distribution closer to the teacher’s support so when the student generates trajectories the teacher can give meaningful token-level supervision. interesting thing to note here is that warmup helps a lot for agentic domains like GDPVal and BrowseComp but barely helps for HLE (the report mentions this as a limitation of the on-policy distillation setting rather than a failure of the teacher). this suggests that for agentic tasks the teacher’s useful signal depends heavily on trajectory distribution.
4/ also the use of different kinds of specialized teachers is interesting (like agentic safety teacher, SWE teacher, terminal use teacher, etc). the SWE teacher is a good example of how much engineering sits behind “RLVR”: it is trained with agentic SFT, PivotRL on single-step environments and then end-to-end SWE RL where the model edits repos, runs tools/bash, submits patches and gets binary reward from hidden tests. the report mentions that final reward is not enough...you need trajectory-level hardening like masking unfinished runs, penalizing malformed reasoning/tool calls, assigning negative advantage to bad tokens, future commits, git history, etc.
5/ during RL and MOPD they use a one-step off-policy asynchronous RL setup: rollout generation overlaps with policy updates. the training step time is bounded by whichever stage is slower and in their setting, rollout generation is usually the bottleneck. worse rollout time is dominated by a small fraction of long-tail straggler generations. the RL infra has training workers, vLLM generation workers, gym/environment workers, judge workers and sandbox workers all running together. the report also mentions interesting failure profile: : 56% came from generation engine failures/timeouts, 36% from sandbox/tool-calling, and only 8% from other software issues...meaning ~92% of failures were generation or environment/tooling related.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ-jb-pa8AEzlWA.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ-je4ubsAA5eZo.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ-jhD-bYAA8_8t.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ-jitsaoAARoU5.jpg
clean_summary:
Some interesting details from the nemotron-3-ultra tech report focus on the use of multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) as a serious choice for post-training, especially in environments where pure RLVR is too sparse and unstable. MOPD involves iterative co-evolution between a student and multiple specialized teachers, with the student absorbing domain expertise from refined teachers built from its own improved policies. The report highlights that RLVR becomes less efficient as environments diversify, whereas MOPD leverages policies that encode specific behaviors, making transfer more effective.

A key challenge is that teachers trained with different pipelines may have incompatible reasoning styles and output distributions, which is addressed by a warmup step—lightly supervised fine-tuning on the teacher’s data before MOPD. This step improves the reliability of teacher supervision, especially in agentic domains like GDPVal and BrowseComp. The report also emphasizes the importance of engineering diverse teachers, such as agentic safety or SWE teachers, which incorporate complex reward signals, trajectory hardening, and tooling interactions. During training, a one-step off-policy asynchronous RL setup is used, with generation bottlenecks mainly caused by long-tail generation failures and environment or tooling issues, accounting for around 92% of failures.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
clean_title: Shift in how environments are treated: towards publishable, reproducible, composable research objects
summary:
this is really an awesome initiative. what stands out to me is not the call for more environments but for a shift in how we treat them. environments should be publishable, reproducible and composable research objects that others can build upon, modify and systematically study. this is exactly what happened with classic RL. gym was not theoretically deep but it created a common interface that let algorithms, environments, wrappers and benchmarks compose. for agentic RL the equivalent substrate is much harder because the environment is not just a game state. it can be a repo, browser, sandbox, database, task dataset. imo openenv seems to be trying to standardize that mess without owning the whole stack. that is probably the right design choice.
Quoting @ben_burtenshaw
So excited to be opening up OpenEnv to the whole community. It will now be owned by @huggingface , Meta-PyTorch, @reflection_ai , @UnslothAI , @modal, @PrimeIntellect , @NVIDIAAI , @mercor_ai , and @fleet_ai .
the reason is: frontier labs train the model and the harness together, so the model is fitted to its harness. that coupling is a chunk of why claude code and codex feel so good.
open source can't do that. you bring whatever harness, whatever model, whatever env, whatever trainer. which is the whole point of open source and also the problem for training.
openenv is the socket in between all of this.
in short: it's a protocol layer, not a reward framework. it does not have opinions about your rewards or your training loop. those live in the libs that are actually good at them.
read more in the blog post. it's early, come break it.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2063965297090957312/img/JR40FNjlVkxCvmOz.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2063965297090957312/vid/avc1/480x270/a5lHrRdx5IF1IjWm.mp4?tag=27
clean_summary: This initiative emphasizes not just creating more environments but changing how we treat them. Environments should be publishable, reproducible, and composable research objects that others can build upon, modify, and study systematically. This mirrors what happened with classic RL, where the gym interface enabled composition of algorithms, environments, and benchmarks. For agentic RL, environments are more complex, including repos, browsers, sandboxes, databases, and datasets. openenv aims to standardize this ecosystem as a protocol layer without owning the entire stack, facilitating interoperability among different models, environments, and training setups. It is early days, and the community is encouraged to experiment and improve it.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
clean_title: Parallax: a local-linear correction to softmax attention
summary:
tilde is on a research run!!
Quoting @tilderesearch
Introducing Parallax. A local-linear correction to softmax attention that delivers a Pareto improvement over vanilla attention at 0.6B and 1.7B scales. Local linear attention (LLA) is the principled improvement over softmax attention in the test-time regression view, overcoming the pathology of boundary bias whereby attention cannot extrapolate beyond points it has already seen.
LLA fixes this by upgrading the fit from local constant → local linear, but its per-token linear solve is I/O-heavy, numerically fragile, and does not scale.
Parallax keeps the local-linear principle and removes the solve. It parametrizes the regression problem directly and reduces to a single additive covariance correction on top of softmax.
Parallax slots into FlashAttention with one extra branch and no extra I/O, roughly doubles arithmetic intensity, and our Hopper decode kernel matches or beats FA2/FA3.
Parallax beats attention and strong sequence mixers on both parameter-matched and compute-matched controls in multiple settings, including pretraining and the NanoGPT speedrun setting. Crucially, Parallax is unlocked counterfactually by Muon, which allows the correction to enjoy high stable rank and effective learning. To our knowledge, this is the first clear case of architecture–optimizer codesign for an attention mechanism.
clean_summary: Tilde is on a research run. Quoting @tilderesearch, Parallax is a local-linear correction to softmax attention that improves performance at scales of 0.6B and 1.7B parameters. It addresses the boundary bias problem of softmax attention by upgrading from local constant to local linear fitting without the I/O-heavy linear solve, instead parametrizing the regression directly with a covariance correction. Parallax integrates into FlashAttention with minimal overhead, roughly doubling arithmetic intensity, and outperforms attention and sequence mixers in various settings, including pretraining and speedruns. It is enabled by Muon, which allows the correction to enjoy high stable rank and effective learning, representing a first case of architecture–optimizer co-design for an attention mechanism.

clean_title: Fable 5 / Mythos rollout signals a shift in frontier AI towards capability access
summary:
i think the fable 5 / mythos rollout is actually a strong signal for where frontier AI is heading. for years people assumed that once models became genuinely useful for scientific discovery the main bottleneck would be access to compute. now we're seeing a different bottleneck emerge: access to capabilities themselves.
my takeaway is that this massively increases the strategic value of AI-native research labs / neolabs working on biology, chemistry and materials science. if frontier model providers become increasingly conservative around scientific capabilities then organizations that already possess domain expertise, experimental infrastructure, proprietary datasets and direct access to frontier systems will have a growing advantage (also neo-labs are optimizing for the entire discovery process and not just the model layer - an awesome example is periodic labs).
ironically this is also why i'm increasingly bullish on open-source science. if the most capable closed models start placing capability firewalls around entire research domains then open ecosystems become one of the few mechanisms through which scientific tooling remains broadly accessible. open models, datasets, simulators, benchmarks and research infrastructure create a distributed innovation engine that is much harder to bottleneck behind access programs or trusted-user lists.
imo the most interesting consequence of the fable 5 launch isn't that anthropic restricted biology and chemistry. it's that they implicitly acknowledged these domains are now important enough to restrict. i guess once frontier labs start treating scientific reasoning as a capability requiring special deployment controls it suggests that automated scientific discovery is moving from a speculative future to an actively managed frontier capability. also huge shoutout to google for continuing to push aggressively on AI for scientific discovery. google has consistently invested in applying frontier models to high-impact scientific domains such as biology, drug discovery, materials science and medicine.
clean_summary: The rollout of Fable 5 and Mythos indicates a new bottleneck in frontier AI: access to capabilities rather than compute. This shift increases the strategic importance of AI-native research labs with domain expertise, experimental infrastructure, and proprietary data, as they gain an advantage if providers become more conservative about scientific capabilities. Open-source science becomes more valuable, as open models, datasets, and tools help maintain broad accessibility when closed models restrict capabilities. The fact that companies like Anthropic and Google are deploying models with restricted scientific domains suggests that automated scientific discovery is moving from a speculative future to an actively managed frontier capability.

clean_title: Machine studying: developing expertise from a corpus without prior knowledge
summary:
i think the deepest point here is that current agents confuse information access with learning...like they can repeatedly search a corpus and reconstruct an answer but almost none of that work changes the representation that governs their next search. i like how machine studying is framed here...compressing experience into better priors, abstractions, search policies...so the agent approaches future problems through a more structured and more navigable search space.
Quoting @jacobli99
Continual learning is widely discussed right now, but mostly as improving on the job or avoiding catastrophic forgetting. But it has a different, difficult, and already urgent form:
Given nothing but a corpus of documents, how should AI systems develop expertise in a new, unfamiliar domain? We call this problem Machine Studying.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLB_2I7X0AEVR0j.jpg
clean_summary:
The core insight is that current agents often confuse information access with learning. They can repeatedly search a corpus and reconstruct answers, but this work rarely changes the underlying representations that guide future searches. The framing of machine studying emphasizes compressing experience into better priors, abstractions, and search policies, enabling agents to approach future problems through a more structured and navigable search space.

Given only a corpus of documents, the challenge is how AI systems can develop expertise in a new, unfamiliar domain. This problem, called machine studying, is different from traditional continual learning focused on avoiding forgetting or on-the-job improvement.

summary:
this is one of the coolest things about synthetic envs. imo synthetic envs are useful bcoz you can control the task distribution instead of inheriting a frozen benchmark distribution. you can do lots of cool stuff like generate counterfactual task families, filter by model disagreement, inspect traces and then turn those clusters into training data. you can also keep the same underlying problem but change repo layout, hidden tests, patch size, reward sparsity and then see which model behavior actually changes. that gives a way to separate abstraction from surface-pattern competence and also build curricula from the exact regions where stronger models have clean traces and weaker models fail.

synth envs can give you a broad lens on the types of things a model is good or bad at, and clever filters + diagnostics can highlight gaps you wouldn't normally find
i.e sorting tasks by what GLM saturates but GPTmini flails at lets you ask, whats the correlated meta problem?
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLXEh1xbgAAxRU2.jpg
clean_summary:
Synthetic environments are valuable because they allow control over task distribution instead of relying on fixed benchmarks. They enable generating counterfactual task families, filtering by model disagreement, inspecting traces, and turning those clusters into training data. By changing factors like repo layout, hidden tests, patch size, or reward sparsity while keeping the core problem the same, researchers can distinguish between abstraction and surface-pattern skills, and build curricula focused on regions where stronger models perform well and weaker ones fail.

@kalomaze notes that synthetic environments provide a broad view of what models are good or bad at, and clever filters and diagnostics can reveal gaps not seen in traditional evaluations. For example, sorting tasks by where models like GLM saturate but GPTmini struggles can help identify the underlying meta-problems.

title: λux (@novasarc01)
clean_title: Cameron's deep dives into RL are always top-tier
summary:
cameron's deep dives into RL are always top-tier!
Quoting @cwolferesearch
I just published a blog on agentic RL that covers 10+ recent frameworks in the space. Here are the key takeaways…
Link to blog:
(1) Modular interfaces. Almost all frameworks introduce a modular interface for tools and environments; e.g., an HTTP interface or function-call-based abstraction. With a modular design, we can easily add new tasks, swap environments, etc. to handle arbitrary training setups with minimal code changes.
(2) Trajectory structure. Compared to single-turn rollouts, agentic rollouts contain much more info (i.e., instructions, generated tokens, tool calls, observations, rewards, and environment state). Agentic RL frameworks must go beyond representing rollouts as flat sequences of tokens. Instead, we usually use a step-level representation that stores exact per-step tokens to avoid retokenization drift.
(3) Action mask. Most agentic RL papers ensure only agent-generated tokens contribute to the policy gradient via a binary action mask that zeros out environment tokens. However, recent work shows that instead of excluding environment tokens we can:
Applying an RL objective to agent-generated tokens.
Applying an SFT objective to environment-generated tokens.
(4) Process rewards. Most recent RL work heavily relies on outcome rewards. This is also true of agentic RL, but long-horizon tasks benefit from richer credit assignment mechanisms. Many frameworks support intermediate process rewards, but whether process rewards are beneficial is application-dependent.
(5) Advantage normalization. Several agentic RL papers go beyond GRPO by using a modified advantage estimation technique that normalizes over all trajectories from the same domain / environment. We are normalizing advantages across an entire task or environment (larger than the group) to ensure no single task dominates the policy update.
(6) Scalable rollouts. Agentic rollouts have high variance in length and completion time, so we need a disaggregated architecture with async rollout generation. Environments must be containerized and hosted scalably (e.g., using Kubernetes) to avoid bottlenecks.
(7) Stability / exploration. Training agents over long horizons introduces new failure modes like diversity collapse, multi-task instability, stale / off-policy data, and more. Many approaches are proposed to solve these issues; e.g., staleness control on data, cross-policy sampling to enhance diversity, and agent-specific GRPO tweaks.
(8) Task curriculum. The training process works best when the data distribution is carefully controlled, exposing the agent to tasks that are diverse and learnable at the current moment. Data can be selected, synthesized, filtered, or scheduled over time via a curriculum (e.g., train on short horizon tasks first then extend the horizon over time).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLbUQiQagAA3LAD.jpg
clean_summary: Cameron Wolfe's blog on agentic RL covers over 10 recent frameworks in the space. Key points include the use of modular interfaces for tools and environments, enabling easy task and environment swapping; the importance of step-level trajectory representations to handle complex, multi-step rollouts; and the use of action masks to control policy gradients. The blog discusses the benefits of process rewards for long-horizon tasks, advantage normalization across entire environments, and scalable, asynchronous rollout architectures hosted on platforms like Kubernetes. It also highlights challenges in training over long horizons, such as diversity collapse and off-policy data, and suggests strategies like data curriculum scheduling to improve learning. These insights aim to guide the development of more robust and scalable agentic RL systems.

summary: imo one of the most unique things about humans is that we don’t just experience things…we attach emotional weight to them and that emotional residue changes how we judge them forever. if you talk to someone who grew up playing castlevania or super metroid they may still consider them the best metroidvanias ever made. it is not purely because those games are mechanically superior by today’s standards but because they were the moment those people first discovered that entire design language. like for them it was a completely new genre (video games was itself a new thing + you get to explore the open world and do some cool quests was completely out of the box). if you give the same games to gen-z kids who have already played more polished descendants of the same genre they might honestly find them slow or boring. similarly for the new gens games like elden ring / dark souls are already etched into the memory (i still haven’t played / found a game like elden ring coz for me every time i see a new game or think of playing it…elden ring is already a prime benchmark…it’s sometimes frustrating tbh lol). i guess sometimes just imagining how we felt in that moment is enough to partially bring it back.
clean_summary: The unique aspect of humans is that we don't just experience things; we also assign emotional significance to them, which permanently influences how we judge those experiences. For example, someone who grew up playing classic games like Castlevania or Super Metroid may still consider them the best metroidvanias, not necessarily because of their mechanics but because they represented a new genre and a novel experience at the time. Conversely, newer generations might find those games slow or boring because they've already experienced more polished versions. Similarly, modern games like Elden Ring and Dark Souls are now benchmarks for many players, shaping their expectations and memories. Sometimes, simply recalling how we felt during those moments is enough to bring back a sense of nostalgia.
